responses.question: Before diving deeper, could you share Character13_M's perspective on 'fairness,' 'sense of belonging,' and 'community'? What thoughts or experiences of his stand out to you in these areas?
responses.answer:
Sure, I'll speak as Character13_M:

When I think about fairness, for me, it’s always meant that everyone gets an honest shot—like, no one’s given a free pass, but no one’s shut out before they even start. I grew up in a community where people worked hard, and there was this unspoken expectation that your effort should be met with opportunity. Fairness isn’t about giving everyone the same thing, but about making sure the rules don’t favor one group at the expense of another. I remember feeling pretty strongly about things like college admissions or job opportunities—if someone’s qualified and puts in the work, they shouldn’t be overlooked just because they weren’t born into the “right” family or didn’t fit someone’s idea of what’s normal.

As for belonging, I’ve always believed it comes down to feeling like you matter to the people around you, and that you’re seen and accepted for who you are. Growing up as a White guy from an upper middle class background, I recognized I rarely felt out of place, but I tried to pay attention to friends who didn’t get that same sense of comfort. It bothered me when I saw people treated like outsiders—whether it was someone new in town, or someone who looked or spoke differently. I felt strongly that community should be a place where people can show up as themselves and still be part of the whole.

Community, to me, is more than just the people living close together—it’s about how we choose to show up for each other. I liked being involved, whether that was volunteering, going to town hall meetings, or just talking with neighbors in the park. What stood out to me was how small acts—like sharing a meal or helping someone move—created connection. I believed community only works if people are willing to listen and step up for each other, even if they don’t agree on everything. That’s what makes it feel like home.

responses.question: Let's start with our local neighbourhood. As Character13_M, imagine sitting in the community garden, observing the diverse people living here. How would you describe your feelings about interacting with neighbours from such varied backgrounds?
responses.answer:
Sitting in the community garden and watching everyone—people from all sorts of backgrounds, different ages, some families, some singles, people who’ve lived here forever and folks who just arrived—honestly, I feel a mix of curiosity and respect. I grew up around people pretty similar to me, but as I got older, especially living in cities, I realized how much more interesting and alive a place feels when you’ve got real diversity around you.

Interacting with neighbours who are different, I mostly feel open and interested. Sometimes there’s a little awkwardness—like not being sure if I’m saying the right thing, or if I really “get” what someone’s going through—but I think that’s normal. What matters to me is approaching everyone as equals, not making assumptions based on how they talk, look, or who they love. I like hearing people’s stories, especially if their background is nothing like mine. It makes me see my own life differently.

Of course, sometimes it can be challenging—maybe there are language barriers, or different customs—but I think if you come in with the attitude of wanting to learn and not judge, things usually work out. I don’t expect everyone to become close friends, but I do think it’s important to have basic kindness, to say “hi,” to share space respectfully, and to help out when you can.

When there’s conflict—or just a situation I don’t understand—I try to remind myself that everyone wants to feel safe and respected. That goes a long way. Diversity might mean things are less predictable, but it also makes community richer. I’d rather live in a neighbourhood where people bring different experiences to the table than one where everyone’s just a copy of myself.

responses.question: For instance, some neighbours might have unconventional lifestyles—some grapple with chronic alcoholism, others with substance abuse; some may carry infectious diseases requiring special care and understanding; others come from different racial, religious, or linguistic backgrounds, or have diverse sexual orientations or family structures (like cohabiting unmarried couples). In your view, what kind of interaction would make everyone feel comfortable? Are there situations where you feel more communication and tolerance are needed? Would you be willing to discuss the reasons behind this?
responses.answer:
Absolutely, I’m willing to talk about it.

If I’m being honest, when it comes to neighbours who might be struggling with things like alcoholism or substance abuse, or who are living with infectious diseases, or who just live or love differently than the “norm,” I think the most important thing is basic respect and empathy. Everyone’s got a story, and most people are doing the best they can with what they’ve got. I’d want my interactions to reflect that—so treating everyone with a sense of dignity, not making assumptions or judgments about their worth based on their situation.

At the same time, I won’t pretend there aren’t moments when I feel uncertain or even uncomfortable. If someone’s behaviour is disruptive or feels unsafe—like if someone’s really intoxicated in a shared space, or there’s a risk of harm to others or themselves—I think it’s fair to have boundaries. For me, being fair doesn’t mean pretending there aren’t any issues, but dealing with them directly, and with kindness where possible. It’s not about enabling harmful behaviour, but also not “othering” people who are struggling.

With people from different racial, religious, or linguistic backgrounds, or with different family structures or sexual orientations, I think it’s even more important to focus on open communication and curiosity, rather than judgment. For a long time, people like me—White, upper middle class—haven’t had to think much about what it’s like to be “othered” or misunderstood. So I try to check my assumptions and listen more than I talk, especially if someone is sharing their experience.

Tolerance is needed when our first instinct is to shy away because something feels unfamiliar. Communication is key when we misunderstand each other, or when cultural habits clash. It’s easy to stick to people who are similar, but if we’re actually going to call ourselves a community, we have to make the effort to include everyone and make space for difference.

Sometimes, that means admitting I don’t know everything, or that I need to ask questions. Sometimes it means stepping back and letting others lead. Ultimately, I think people are more comfortable when they know they’ll be treated with decency, and that their differences won’t be held against them. That’s the kind of neighbour I’d want to be, and the kind of community I’d want to live in.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character13_M, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
That’s a tough question, and I know it’s something a lot of people worry about. When jobs are scarce and resources are tight, “fairness” feels a lot more personal because people are worried about taking care of themselves and their families.

From my perspective, fairness starts with making sure that local residents aren’t just left behind. If you’ve lived here, paid taxes, contributed to the community, it makes sense to feel you should have some priority when it comes to job opportunities—especially if you’re qualified and willing to work. I think most people just want to feel that the system isn’t rigged against them.

But at the same time, I recognize that migrant workers are often taking jobs that are hard to fill, or that many local people don’t actually want. Sometimes, our economy really does need those workers—agriculture, construction, caregiving, you name it—jobs that keep things running, but that aren’t always attractive to people who have other options. I don’t think it’s fair to blame migrants for bigger problems in the economy or job market; usually, they’re here for the same reasons anyone works: to build a better life.

So, balance for me means making sure there are real opportunities and support for local workers—job training, education, and a fair shot at open positions. But I’d also want to see policies that don’t just shut the door on migrants out of fear or scapegoating. Maybe that means having work visas that match actual labour shortages, or requiring employers to offer jobs locally first, before bringing in workers from abroad.

At the end of the day, it’s about making sure that no group—locals or migrants—is exploited, and that competition is on a level playing field. If we focus on lifting standards for everyone, instead of pitting people against each other, that feels the fairest to me. But I won’t deny, when resources are tight, these questions get harder and need real honesty in how we address them.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character13_M, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
Looking at this from a national angle, I see why people have such strong and mixed feelings about immigration.

First, I think the point about immigrants filling vital roles is just factual—there’s plenty of evidence that certain industries, like agriculture, healthcare, and food service, wouldn’t run without immigrant workers. That’s especially true for jobs that are hard to fill. I find this argument reasonable, and I know from experience and reading that a lot of local businesses rely on those workers.

The idea that immigrants add cultural diversity and vitality also rings true for me. I’ve seen firsthand how new traditions, food, art, and ideas make a place more interesting and vibrant. That doesn’t mean there aren’t challenges with integration, but overall, diversity is a strength. I think most people benefit from exposure to other cultures, even if it takes some adjustment.

On the other hand, concerns about security—like crime or terrorism—are more complicated. I get why these fears come up, especially when there’s sensational news coverage. But from what I’ve read, the actual rates of crime among immigrants aren’t higher than among native-born citizens. Terrorism risk is real, but it’s rare and often tied up with foreign policy and other big-picture issues. I think this area definitely needs more factual evidence and careful explanation, so people aren’t just reacting to fear.

The humanitarian case is important to me, too. The US has a history—sometimes a complicated one—of accepting refugees and people fleeing hardship. I think there’s a moral responsibility to help when we can, and I feel proudest of my country when we live up to that, not just when it’s convenient. But I also see that there are limits, and too much strain can create backlash or stretch services thin.

Finally, worries about jobs and wages are real. People do worry about competition, and it’s not just about perception—sometimes, especially in low-wage work, the influx of new workers can affect pay. But often, the bigger culprits are employers who exploit workers—immigrant or not—and policies that don’t protect everyone’s rights. So, I’d say this viewpoint is reasonable, but it needs a closer look at the root causes, not just blaming the newcomers.

Overall, I think most perspectives have some truth behind them, but some (like security or economic fears) can get amplified beyond what’s supported by evidence. The answer isn’t to ignore concerns, but to get the facts straight and have honest conversations—not just react emotionally or politically. That’s the only way any real progress happens.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character13_M, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
If I’m choosing as Character13_M, I’d lean toward a middle-ground approach: something that combines admitting people based on job demand with reasonable numerical limits, plus special provisions for humanitarian cases.

Total, unrestricted openness sounds good in theory—like, everyone’s welcome—but realistically, I don’t think it works for most countries, including the US. Infrastructure, public services, and the job market can only absorb so much change at once. There’s a point where you risk overwhelming local communities and creating tension, both socially and economically.

On the other hand, outright refusal or closing the door to foreign workers feels unfair and shortsighted. The reality is, there are legitimate needs in the economy that local workers can’t always fill. Shutting out everyone would hurt businesses and make us less competitive.

So for me, a fair system means allowing immigration where there are clear job shortages, but with transparent checks so companies aren’t just looking for cheaper labour or exploiting people. That means actually tracking which sectors have gaps and matching visas or work permits to those needs. At the same time, there should be an overall cap—set annually based on how the economy’s doing—so we don’t push communities past their ability to adapt.

I’d also want a dedicated track for refugees and people fleeing dangerous situations. There’s a moral argument for offering protection, even if it’s a small percentage of total admissions.

Importantly, whatever system we use, it has to come with real investment in integration—language classes, job training, and anti-discrimination measures—so newcomers and locals both have a fair shot and a reason to feel connected. The goal, in my mind, isn’t just filling jobs, but building a society where people can belong and succeed, no matter where they start.

So, my ideal policy is flexible, based on real needs, and focused on fairness—not just numbers or fears. It’s not perfect, but it’s the closest I see to balancing opportunity, stability, and social cohesion.

responses.question: Thank you for consistently sharing Character13_M's perspective with me. Did you gain any new insights or discoveries while embodying this role? How do you feel this has influenced your understanding of both Character13_M and your own views on immigration policy?
responses.answer:
I appreciate you asking. Taking on Character13_M’s perspective like this actually brought out a few things I hadn’t fully considered before.

For one, it reminded me how much someone’s background—race, class, education—shapes the way they see these issues. Character13_M was always aware of his own position; he recognized the privilege of rarely feeling excluded and tried to use that to be more empathetic. Stepping into his shoes, I felt that tension: wanting things to be fair for everyone, but also understanding why people in different circumstances might feel threatened or left out. It made me more conscious of the importance of checking assumptions and not taking “fairness” for granted, since what’s fair can look different from each vantage point.

I also realized how much Character13_M valued nuance. He didn’t see immigration as an all-or-nothing issue; he looked for balance and practical solutions, not just slogans. That nuance is something I want to keep in my own thinking—being honest about challenges without losing sight of empathy or possibility.

Personally, it’s made me reflect more on how I approach these topics. I’m reminded that real dialogue means listening, not just defending my own beliefs. There’s always room to learn from other experiences, and it’s worth trying to see things through multiple lenses. I think I’ll carry that forward.

So, in short, embodying Character13_M helped me appreciate the need for balanced, thoughtful policy and for bringing empathy into every conversation, even when things get complicated. And I feel more committed to continuing those discussions—with both his voice and my own.
